body: Wirecard, a German payments processor in the DAX, peaked near EUR 190 in Sep 2018 (market cap ~EUR 24 bn). On 18 Jun 2020 auditor EY said EUR 1.9 bn of cash in Philippine trustee accounts could not be confirmed; on 22 Jun the company admitted it probably did not exist; CEO Markus Braun was arrested; insolvency on 25 Jun 2020; shares fell >98%. Visible flags years ahead: (1) FT Alphaville 'House of Wirecard' (2015) and Zatarra report (2016) questioned Asian acquisitions; (2) about half of profits came via 'third-party acquirers' (TPAs) in Asia that Wirecard did not control; (3) acquisitions at inflated prices (e.g., ~EUR 340 m for Indian assets in 2015, much of it to a Mauritius fund); (4) operating cash flow far weaker than EBITDA once customer-fund movements were stripped out; rising receivables; (5) FT's Dan McCrum's Jan 2019 whistleblower-based reports on Singapore round-tripping; (6) KPMG special audit (Apr 2020) could not verify revenues. Instead, BaFin banned short-selling (Feb-Apr 2019) and filed complaints against FT journalists. Lesson: regulator defence and DAX membership are not evidence; when profits sit in partners you can't audit and cash is held by 'trustees', require independent confirmation. Short sellers and journalists were right for 5 years.

data.early_signals: TPA-sourced profits; trustee-held cash; overpriced Asian acquisitions; EBITDA >> CFO; FT reporting; KPMG non-verification
data.spotted_by: Dan McCrum (FT), Zatarra, short sellers (e.g., Fraser Perring)

title: Wirecard (2020): EUR 1.9 bn cash that didn't exist
